summary: For ages 6–8, teach that organisms live in habitats suited to them because each habitat feature supplies a specific basic need (food, water, shelter, suitable conditions), and that living things depend on each other, not only on the place. The central move is causal need→feature matching plus predicting failure when a need is unmet, rather than matching animal to place by appearance. Plants, like animals, have needs met by a habitat. Interdependence is introduced concretely with a mutual organism pair before any abstract 'web' language.
misconceptions: Matching animal to habitat by appearance or familiarity, without linking to needs.
Thinking any animal could survive anywhere if it 'tried'.
Seeing organisms as independent — missing that they depend on each other, not just on the physical place.
Believing plants don't have needs or a habitat in the same sense as animals.
Treating 'habitat' as only the shelter/home rather than the whole life-supporting place.

activities.title: Build-a-habitat: match every need to a feature
steps: Place an organism (e.g. a frog) into different habitats — pond, desert, woodland — and for each one go through a four-item needs checklist: food, water, shelter, suitable conditions.
For each need, name the specific habitat feature that supplies it, or mark it unmet: e.g. 'the pond gives the frog water, insects to eat, and reeds to hide in.'

Also work a plant case: place pond weed and ask whether it could move to the desert — name which needs (water, suitable conditions) the desert fails, so plants are seen to have needs and a habitat just as animals do.
Predict out loud what happens when a need is unmet — e.g. a pond frog in a dry desert has no pond water and no damp place to keep its skin moist, so it cannot survive there.
Finally, design a suitable home for a new creature and defend it need-by-need, stating which feature meets each need.
activities.insight: 'Suited to' means every basic need is met by something in the habitat; an organism placed where a need cannot be met cannot survive. Suitability is a causal consequence, not decoration or appearance. Plants as well as animals have needs met by their habitat.

activities.title: Depend on each other: the mutual pair
steps: Study a mutual-dependence pair of living things — bee and flower — and state what each gives the other (bees pollinate flowers so they make seeds/fruit; flowers feed bees).
Trace one dependency chain in a pond — pond plants feed insects, insects feed the frog — and say which organism relies on which.

Explore 'remove the bees' as a thought-experiment: flowers that rely on bees to carry their pollen would make fewer seeds and fruit, so an animal that fed on those seeds or fruit could lose some of its food. Say which need flips to unmet and why. (Some plants, like grasses, are pollinated by the wind instead, and other animals besides bees can also pollinate.)
Name one thing the frog gives back to the pond, not just what it takes, to see dependence running both ways.

(Extension) Note that a worm also depends on its soil habitat — the soil gives it food and shelter and the worm enriches the soil — but recognise soil is part of the habitat, not another living partner like the bee and flower.
activities.insight: Living things depend on each other, not only on the physical place; removing one organism can take away another organism's met need. Interdependence between organisms is a concrete relationship before it is an abstract 'web.'

activities.title: Talk it through as the organism
steps: Take the role of an organism: 'I'm a frog — what do I need, and where in my habitat do I get each thing?'
Have a partner (or the learner) propose a different home for the creature, then say which specific need would fail there and why.
Transfer to a new case: a woodlouse lives under a damp log — say what would happen to it on a hot, dry path and which need (damp shelter/suitable conditions) fails.
Say aloud a full explanation: name each need, the feature that meets it, and at least one way the organism depends on another organism.
activities.insight: Being able to say, in your own words, which need each feature meets and which need a wrong place fails shows the matching is understood, not memorised, and transfers to new organisms.

activities.title: Check and score: which need fails?
steps: Match organisms to habitats, then answer a follow-up that asks WHICH need fails in a wrong pairing — e.g. 'Why can't a cactus live in a pond?' or 'Why can't a fish live on the sand?'
Sort features of a habitat by which need they meet (food, water, shelter, conditions).
Answer: 'A frog lives in a pond. It is moved to a dry, sunny field with no water. Will it be okay — and what exactly did the pond give that the field does not?'
activities.insight: A correct answer names the specific needs the new place fails to provide; treating places as interchangeable or naming no need signals a misconception.

checkQuestion: Tell the child: 'A frog lives in a pond. I scoop it up and move it to a dry, sunny field where there is no water.' Ask: 'Will the frog be okay there? Why or why not — and what exactly did the pond give the frog that the field does not?'
checkAnswer: The frog will not be okay. A habitat provides everything an organism needs: the pond gave water (to keep its skin moist and to breathe/live in), food such as insects, and shelter. The dry field meets none of these, so the frog cannot survive. A good answer names specific needs the new place fails to provide.
